questions.stem: What does a mechanical wave transfer from one place to another?
options: The medium itself, carried along at the wave speed
Both energy and the medium, at the same speed
Charge, which moves through the medium as a current
Energy, without any net transfer of the medium
questions.explanation: A wave is a travelling disturbance. Each particle of the medium oscillates about a fixed position, while the energy moves on. A floating cork bobs up and down as water waves pass but is not carried along with them.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a transverse wave from a longitudinal wave?
options: A transverse wave needs a medium, while a longitudinal wave does not
A transverse wave carries energy, while a longitudinal wave carries matter
In a transverse wave the particles oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel
In a transverse wave the particles oscillate along the direction of travel
questions.explanation: The two types are defined by how the oscillation is oriented relative to the wave's velocity: perpendicular for transverse waves, parallel for longitudinal waves. Both carry energy, and mechanical waves of either type need a medium.

questions.stem: Which description of a sound wave travelling through air is correct?
options: A transverse mechanical wave of crests and troughs
A longitudinal electromagnetic wave that can cross a vacuum
A transverse electromagnetic wave of oscillating fields
A longitudinal mechanical wave of compressions and rarefactions
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave: air molecules oscillate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming regions of higher pressure (compressions) and lower pressure (rarefactions). It needs a medium, so it cannot cross a vacuum.

questions.stem: Light from the Sun reaches Earth, but sound from the Sun does not. Which property of light explains this?
options: It is an electromagnetic wave, so it can travel through a vacuum
It is a longitudinal wave, so it needs no medium
It travels much faster than sound, so it arrives before fading
It has a much higher amplitude than any sound wave
questions.explanation: Light is an electromagnetic wave with transverse qualities, made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, and needs no medium. Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot cross the near-vacuum of space, however fast or loud it is.

questions.stem: As a wave passes, each particle of the medium oscillates in simple harmonic motion. Where in its oscillation is a particle moving fastest?
options: At its maximum displacement
Halfway between equilibrium and maximum displacement
Its speed is the same at all points
At its equilibrium position
questions.explanation: In simple harmonic motion the restoring force, and so the acceleration, is greatest at maximum displacement, where the particle momentarily stops. It speeds up towards equilibrium and moves fastest as it passes through it.

questions.stem: A tuning fork vibrating at 440 Hz produces sound in air, where its speed is 343 m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = v/f = 343/440 ≈ 0.78 m. Dividing f by v gives 1.28, which has units of per metre, and multiplying gives an absurdly large wavelength.

questions.stem: A wave has a period of 0.025 s and a wavelength of 0.50 m. What is its speed?
options: 40 m s⁻¹
20 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: f = 1/T = 1/0.025 = 40 Hz, so v = fλ = 40 × 0.50 = 20 m s⁻¹. Multiplying the period by the wavelength gives 0.0125, which skips converting period to frequency, and 40 is the frequency, not the speed.

questions.stem: A wave passes from one medium into another in which it travels more slowly. Which quantity stays the same?
options: Its speed
Its direction, whatever the angle of incidence
Its frequency
Its wavelength
questions.explanation: Frequency is set by the source; each crest arriving at the boundary produces one crest on the other side, so frequency cannot change. Since v = fλ, a lower speed means a shorter wavelength. The direction changes unless the wave meets the boundary head-on.

questions.stem: In a sound wave in air, a compression and the nearest rarefaction are 0.85 m apart. The frequency is 200 Hz. What is the speed of sound?
options: 170 m s⁻¹
680 m s⁻¹
235 m s⁻¹
340 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: A compression and the next rarefaction are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 1.70 m and v = fλ = 200 × 1.70 = 340 m s⁻¹. Treating 0.85 m as a whole wavelength gives 170 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: Two points on a travelling wave are exactly half a wavelength apart. How are their motions related?
options: One is always at a crest while the other is always at equilibrium
They are unrelated, because the wave is travelling
They are always moving in opposite directions, with equal and opposite displacements
They are always moving in the same direction, with the same displacement
questions.explanation: Points half a wavelength apart are 180° out of phase: when one is at a crest the other is at a trough, and their displacements are always equal and opposite. Points one whole wavelength apart move in step.

questions.stem: A transverse wave travels to the right along a rope. At one instant, point P on the rope is at the top of a crest. Where is P a quarter of a period later?
options: At the top of the next crest to the right
At its equilibrium position, moving upward
At the bottom of a trough
At its equilibrium position, moving downward
questions.explanation: P only moves up and down. From the top of a crest it moves back towards equilibrium, reaching it after a quarter period and continuing downward. The crest itself has moved a quarter of a wavelength to the right, but P has not travelled with it.

questions.stem: A student sends a larger-amplitude pulse along the same stretched rope. Compared with a small pulse, how does it travel?
options: Faster, carrying more energy
At the same speed, carrying the same energy
Slower, because it has more mass to move
At the same speed, carrying more energy
questions.explanation: Wave speed depends on the medium, here the tension and mass per unit length of the rope, not on the amplitude. A larger amplitude means more energy is carried, at the same speed.

questions.stem: A pulse travels along a rope towards an end that is tied firmly to a wall. How is the reflected pulse different from the incoming one?
options: It is upright, showing no phase change
It is inverted and travels faster than the incoming pulse
It is upright but has double the amplitude
It is inverted, showing a phase change of half a cycle
questions.explanation: At a fixed end the rope cannot move, so it pulls down on the wall as the pulse arrives and the wall pulls back, sending an inverted pulse back. This is a phase change of 180°. The speed is unchanged because the medium is the same.

questions.stem: A pulse reaches an end of a string that is free to move, such as a ring sliding on a smooth pole. What is the reflected pulse like?
options: Upright, with no phase change
Inverted, with a phase change of half a cycle
Absent, because all of the energy escapes at a free end
Upright, but travelling more slowly than before
questions.explanation: A free end overshoots as the pulse arrives and then drags the string back, sending back an upright pulse with no phase change. Inversion happens at a fixed end. A pulse is not lost at a free end; it reflects.

questions.stem: A pulse on a light string reaches a junction with a much heavier string. What happens at the junction?
options: All of it is transmitted, slowing down but unchanged in shape
Part is transmitted upright and part is reflected inverted
Part is transmitted inverted and part is reflected upright
All of it is reflected upright, as at a free end
questions.explanation: The heavier string resists motion and behaves like a partly fixed end, so the reflected pulse is inverted. Some energy also passes into the heavy string as an upright pulse travelling more slowly. A junction between different media both reflects and transmits.

questions.stem: A pulse on a heavy rope reaches a junction with a light string. Which statement describes the reflected and transmitted pulses?
options: Both are upright, and the transmitted pulse travels faster
The reflected pulse is inverted and the transmitted one upright
Both are inverted, and the transmitted pulse travels faster
Both are upright, and the transmitted pulse travels more slowly
questions.explanation: The light string offers little resistance, so the junction behaves like a free end and the reflected pulse is upright. The transmitted pulse is also upright, and it moves faster because the light string has a smaller mass per unit length.

questions.stem: A student claps once in front of a cliff and hears the echo 1.2 s later. If sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹, how far away is the cliff?
questions.explanation: The sound travels to the cliff and back, a total of 340 × 1.2 = 408 m, so the cliff is half that, 204 m away. Quoting 408 m forgets that the echo makes a round trip.

questions.stem: How are the angles of incidence and reflection measured when a wave reflects from a surface?
options: From the direction of the reflected wave
From the vertical, whatever the orientation of the surface
From the normal, a line perpendicular to the surface
From the surface itself, along the boundary
questions.explanation: Both angles are measured from the normal at the point where the ray strikes. The law of reflection is θi = θr. Measuring from the surface is a common slip that gives the complement of the correct angle.

questions.stem: A light ray strikes a flat mirror at 25° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, so it is 90° − 25° = 65°. The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, 65°. Quoting 25° measures from the surface, and 130° is the angle between the incident and reflected rays.

questions.stem: What causes a wave to change direction as it crosses a boundary at an angle?
options: Absorption of part of the wave's energy at the boundary
A change in the wave's speed between the two media
A change in the wave's frequency between the two media
Reflection of part of the wave at the boundary
questions.explanation: Refraction happens because the wave travels at a different speed in the second medium. One side of a wavefront changes speed before the other, so the wavefront swings round. Frequency does not change at a boundary.

questions.stem: A light ray passes at an angle from air into glass, where light travels more slowly. How does it bend?
options: It does not bend, since light is not a mechanical wave
Towards the normal
Away from the normal
Along the boundary
questions.explanation: A wave entering a slower medium bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. Leaving glass for air, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.stem: Water waves travel at 0.30 m s⁻¹ in deep water and 0.20 m s⁻¹ in shallow water. What is the refractive index of the shallow water relative to the deep water?
questions.explanation: The relative refractive index is n = sin θi / sin θr = v₁/v₂ = 0.30/0.20 = 1.5, where medium 1 is the deep water the waves come from. The value 0.67 inverts the ratio, and 0.10 is the difference in speeds.

questions.stem: Water waves pass from deep water, where they travel at 0.30 m s⁻¹, into shallow water, where they travel at 0.20 m s⁻¹. They meet the boundary at 40° to the normal. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: sin θr = sin 40° × v₂/v₁ = 0.643 × 0.20/0.30 = 0.429, so θr ≈ 25°. Scaling the angle itself gives 27°, which wrongly treats angles as proportional to their sines. The waves slow down, so they must bend towards the normal, which rules out 60° and 75°.

questions.stem: The absolute refractive index of a type of glass is 1.50. What is the speed of light in it? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The absolute refractive index is the ratio c/v, so v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.50 = 2.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Multiplying gives a speed faster than light in a vacuum, which is impossible.

questions.stem: A light ray in air strikes a glass block of refractive index 1.50 at an angle of incidence of 50°. What is the angle of refraction? Take n for air as 1.00.
questions.explanation: Snell's law: 1.00 × sin 50° = 1.50 × sin θ, so sin θ = 0.766/1.50 = 0.511 and θ ≈ 31°. Dividing the angle itself by 1.50 gives 33°, and 59° is the refracted ray's angle to the surface rather than to the normal.

questions.stem: Light passes from water (n = 1.33) into glass (n = 1.50) at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ gives sin θ₂ = 1.33 × sin 35° / 1.50 = 0.509, so θ₂ ≈ 31°. Swapping the indices gives 40°, which would mean bending away from the normal on entering a slower medium.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass with a refractive index of 1.50. What is its wavelength in the glass?
options: 400 nm
900 nm
600 nm
200 nm
questions.explanation: The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength is reduced in the same ratio as the speed: λ = 600/1.50 = 400 nm. Multiplying gives 900 nm, and keeping 600 nm confuses wavelength with frequency, the quantity that stays the same.

questions.stem: Which conditions are both needed for total internal reflection?
options: The wave travels towards a medium where it is faster, at less than the critical angle
The wave travels towards a medium where it is slower, at less than the critical angle
The wave travels towards a medium where it is faster, at more than the critical angle
The wave travels towards a medium where it is slower, at more than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection can only happen when the wave would bend away from the normal, that is, when moving into a medium where it travels faster. Above the critical angle no refracted wave is possible, and all of the wave is reflected.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light passing from glass of refractive index 1.50 into air?
questions.explanation: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary, so 1.50 × sin c = 1.00 × sin 90° and sin c = 1/1.50, giving c ≈ 42°. The value 48° is 90° minus the answer, and 56° comes from tan⁻¹ 1.50.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle at a boundary between glass (n = 1.50) and water (n = 1.33), for light travelling from the glass?
questions.explanation: sin c = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so c ≈ 62°. The value 42° is the glass-air critical angle and 49° the water-air one. Water's index is closer to glass's, so the critical angle is larger than for glass and air.

questions.stem: How does an optical fibre keep light travelling along it?
options: The cladding has a higher refractive index than the core, which bends the light inward
Light is absorbed by the core and re-emitted further along the fibre
Light totally internally reflects at the boundary between the core and the cladding
A mirror coating on the outside of the fibre reflects light back into the core
questions.explanation: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding. Light meeting the boundary at more than the critical angle is totally internally reflected again and again, staying in the core with little loss. A higher index in the cladding would make total internal reflection impossible.

questions.stem: A light ray in water (n = 1.33) strikes the water's surface from below at 55° to the normal. What happens to it?
options: It travels along the surface, since 55° equals the critical angle
It is totally internally reflected, since 55° exceeds the critical angle of about 49°
It refracts into the air, bending away from the normal
It refracts into the air, bending towards the normal
questions.explanation: The critical angle for water to air is sin⁻¹(1/1.33) ≈ 49°. The ray meets the surface at 55°, more than the critical angle, so no light refracts out and all of it reflects back into the water. Below 49° it would refract out, bending away from the normal.

questions.stem: Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in air and 1500 m s⁻¹ in water. What is the critical angle for sound travelling from air into water?
options: There is none, because water is denser than air
questions.explanation: Sound is faster in water, so it bends away from the normal entering the water and can be totally reflected. sin c = v₁/v₂ = 340/1500 = 0.227, so c ≈ 13°. What matters is the change in wave speed, not density; 77° is the complement of the answer.

questions.stem: Which kind of wave can be polarised?
options: Transverse waves only
Longitudinal waves only
Both transverse and longitudinal waves
Electromagnetic waves only, never mechanical waves
questions.explanation: Polarisation restricts the oscillation to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is only possible for transverse waves. Sound, a longitudinal wave, cannot be polarised, while transverse mechanical waves on a rope can.

questions.stem: Unpolarised light passes through a Polaroid filter and then through a second Polaroid whose transmission axis is at 90° to the first. What emerges from the second filter?
options: Half of the light leaving the first filter
All of the light leaving the first filter
Light polarised at 45° to both filters
No light
questions.explanation: The first filter passes only light oscillating along its axis. The second filter, crossed at 90°, blocks oscillations in that direction completely, so almost no light gets through. This is strong evidence that light is a transverse wave.

questions.stem: Why do polarising sunglasses reduce the glare from the surface of a lake?
options: Reflected light is partly polarised vertically, and the lenses block vertical oscillations
The lenses absorb all light reflected from water, whatever its polarisation
The lenses reflect bright light back towards the lake before it enters the eye
Reflected light is partly polarised horizontally, and the lenses block horizontal oscillations
questions.explanation: Light reflected from water or glass is partly polarised, mostly oscillating parallel to the surface, which for a lake is horizontal. Polarising sunglasses transmit only vertical oscillations, so they cut most of the glare while still letting through light from other objects.

questions.stem: A photographer notices that blue sky at right angles to the Sun's direction looks darker through a rotating polarising filter at one angle. What does this show?
options: Light scattered by the air is partly polarised
Air molecules absorb all light polarised vertically
Sunlight is fully polarised before it enters the atmosphere
The filter is changing the frequency of the light
questions.explanation: Sunlight is unpolarised, but light scattered by air molecules becomes partly polarised, most strongly at 90° to the Sun's direction. Rotating the filter blocks more of that polarised light at one orientation, darkening the sky. A filter does not change frequency.
